subject: 중세 도시의 길드와 기술 전수
title: Guilds and the passing on of medieval craft
content: A medieval guild is often pictured as a body that restricted trade, and its rules about who might work and at what price support that reading. Yet the same rules addressed a problem that no market of the period could solve on its own, namely how a craft was to be learned. Skills that took years to acquire could not be written down in any useful form, so they passed from one pair of hands to another, and the arrangements that made this possible had to be enforced by somebody. The apprenticeship contracts that survive show what was at stake. A master took a boy for a term of years, fed and housed him, and taught him in exchange for labour that was worthless at the start and valuable at the end. Neither side could enforce such a bargain alone, since the boy might leave once he had learned enough and the master might teach him nothing while keeping the labour. The guild stood behind the contract, and its power to exclude a member from the trade was what made the promise credible. This explains why guilds appear wherever medieval crafts were complex and disappear where they were simple. Their restrictive rules and their teaching function were not separable, because the restriction was the enforcement mechanism. Historians who judge them only as monopolies therefore miss what the same institution accomplished, and they cannot explain why the skills survived the centuries during which nothing was written down.

subject: 결과주의와 그 반례들
title: Consequences and the cases that trouble them
content: The moral theory that judges actions by their outcomes has an appeal that is hard to dismiss. It explains why suffering matters, it provides a single standard for hard choices, and it treats everyone's interests as equally weighty. Whatever else morality involves, making things go better seems to be part of it, and any rival theory must explain why it is not the whole. The difficulties arise in a familiar family of cases. Each involves a situation where the best total outcome requires harming an innocent person, and in each our judgment resists what the theory recommends. Transplanting the organs of one healthy patient to save five is the standard illustration, and almost nobody accepts the verdict that the surgeon should proceed. The theory answers that we may keep the intuition as a useful rule while denying that it tracks any deeper truth. That answer has not satisfied its critics. If the intuition is merely a rule of thumb, then a well-informed agent should set it aside when the arithmetic is clear, and the theory offers no reason why he should not. Defenders reply that our confidence in the intuition is itself evidence about morality, so a theory that contradicts it has been refuted rather than merely challenged. What the debate has established is that the disagreement concerns method, since the two sides differ about whether a moral judgment can outweigh a moral argument.

subject: 감자와 옥수수가 바꾼 인구
title: New crops and the growth of populations
content: Two crops carried out of the Americas after the ocean crossings of the sixteenth century changed how many people the Old World could feed. Maize yielded well on land that suited no grain, and the potato produced more calories per unit of ground than any cereal while tolerating cool and wet conditions. Regions that adopted them supported populations that their earlier agriculture could not have sustained, and the demographic records of the following centuries register the change clearly. Adoption was neither quick nor even, and the delays are instructive. Farmers resisted crops they did not know how to store, tax collectors preferred grain they could measure in a granary, and communities suspicious of a plant that grew underground took generations to change. Where landholding was insecure, the potato spread faster, since a crop that could be left in the ground was harder for a landlord or an army to seize. The new plants therefore entered by different doors in different places. The dependence that followed carried its own risk. A population grown on a single crop has no reserve when that crop fails, and the famines of the nineteenth century in regions that had come to rely on the potato demonstrated the cost. Historians read the episode as a warning about narrow subsistence rather than as an argument against the crop, since the same plant had allowed those populations to exist at all.

subject: 처벌의 정당화 근거
title: What justifies punishment
content: Punishment involves deliberately imposing hardship on a person, which ordinarily requires justification of a serious kind. Moral philosophy has offered two broad answers, and each captures something the other misses. The forward-looking answer justifies punishment by its effects, holding that it deters offences, protects the public, and may reform the offender. The backward-looking answer justifies it by desert, holding that a person who has done wrong deserves to suffer for it whatever the consequences. Each answer produces conclusions its defenders would rather avoid. If deterrence justifies punishment, then punishing an innocent person would be justified whenever the public believed him guilty and the deterrent effect were secured, which almost everyone rejects. If desert justifies it, then we must punish even where no good whatever comes of doing so, and the value of that outcome is difficult to articulate without appealing to something the theory rules out. Most contemporary positions combine the two, using desert to set the limits within which consequences may operate. On this view nobody may be punished who does not deserve it, and among those who do, the amount is settled by what will actually help. The combination is more defensible than either alone, though it inherits the burden of explaining why desert constrains without justifying, and that question remains open in the moral literature.

subject: 초원길과 정주 세계의 접촉
title: The steppe and the settled world
content: The grasslands running across ancient Asia supported herders who moved with their animals, and the farming societies to the south often described them as an external threat that arrived without warning. The archaeological record describes a much closer relationship. Goods, animals, and people crossed between the two worlds continuously, and the settlements at the edge show mixed material culture over many centuries rather than a frontier that was occasionally breached. What each side supplied is easy to state. The steppe produced horses and the skills to use them, which no settled society could match on its own terms, while the farming regions produced grain, textiles, and metalwork that the herders wanted and could not make in quantity. Exchange was therefore constant, and raiding was one form it took when exchange broke down rather than an alternative to it. Ancient sources written from the settled side record the raids and omit the trade. The consequences ran both ways. Settled armies adopted cavalry and the equipment that made it effective, while steppe leaders who controlled access to southern markets acquired power over their own followers that pasture alone could not have given them. Historians accordingly treat the ancient steppe and the farming world as one system with two halves, and the events that the chronicles present as invasions usually mark a change in the terms between them.

subject: 관용의 역설
title: The paradox of toleration
content: Toleration is usually praised as a virtue, and yet the concept contains a difficulty that becomes visible as soon as it is stated precisely. To tolerate something is to permit what one judges to be wrong, since a practice one approves of requires no toleration at all. The virtue therefore consists in refraining from acting against what one has good reason to oppose, and that combination is not obviously coherent. If the disapproval is warranted, why should it not be acted upon? Several answers have been offered in moral philosophy. One appeals to fallibility, arguing that our confidence in any judgment should be tempered by the frequency with which such judgments have proved mistaken. A second appeals to autonomy, holding that a person's own direction of her life has a value that outweighs the harm of her choosing badly. A third is practical, observing that the machinery required to suppress a practice usually causes more damage than the practice does. A further difficulty concerns limits. A toleration that extends to everything would include the intolerant, who would then use their freedom to end it, and a toleration that excludes them requires a principle for drawing the line that is not itself an act of intolerance. Most positions accept that some line must be drawn and disagree about where, which means that the practical question is never settled by endorsing the value alone.

subject: 진실을 말할 의무와 해악
title: Truthfulness when the truth will harm
content: A doctor who must tell a patient of a poor prognosis, a friend asked about a painful matter, and an official holding information that would cause panic all face the same moral structure. There is a duty to speak truly and a duty not to cause harm, and in these cases the two point in opposite directions. Moral philosophy has approached the conflict in ways that reveal what each side takes duty to be. One position treats truthfulness as owed to the person addressed rather than to the world, so that what is required is not the disclosure of every fact but the absence of deception. On this view a doctor may choose what to emphasize and when to speak without wronging anyone, provided she creates no false belief. The distinction between withholding and deceiving does real work here, and much medical ethics rests on it. Critics answer that the distinction is easier to state than to apply. A carefully selected truth can mislead as thoroughly as a lie, and the person who arranges the selection knows this. They add that judgments about what another can bear are notoriously self-serving, since they spare the speaker as much as the hearer. What both sides accept is that the person addressed has a claim to govern her own affairs, and that claim is what makes the case difficult rather than merely delicate.

subject: 태평양 항해와 섬의 정착
title: Settling the islands of the Pacific
content: The islands scattered across the Pacific were settled by people who crossed open water in vessels without instruments, reaching landfalls separated by hundreds of miles of empty ocean. For a long time this was explained by accident, with canoes blown off course and survivors landing where they could. The pattern of settlement makes that account untenable, since the movement ran against the prevailing winds and reached islands that no drifting vessel would encounter. What the voyagers used instead has been partly reconstructed. Navigators read the swell, which holds its direction beneath local winds, and they watched the stars rising and setting at known points on the horizon. Birds that return to land at dusk and the reflection of a lagoon on the underside of clouds extended the target far beyond what the eye could reach directly. Sailing into the wind on the outward leg was itself a safety measure, since a failed voyage could return home downwind. Ancient settlement therefore proceeded deliberately, and the archaeological dates show it advancing in stages with long pauses between them. Those pauses are as informative as the movements, because they mark the intervals during which vessels, techniques, or the plants that had to be carried were being developed. What crossed the ocean was not merely a population but a system for reproducing a whole way of living on ground that held none of it.

subject: 가치 다원주의와 비교 불가능성
title: Values that cannot be compared
content: Choosing between two careers, or between a friendship and a duty, often feels unlike weighing two quantities of the same thing. Moral philosophy has therefore asked whether this appearance is accurate, and the question matters because a great deal of practical reasoning assumes that such options can be ranked. If some values genuinely cannot be measured against one another, then rational choice is more limited than we suppose. The argument for incomparability begins with a test. Where two options can be compared, adding a small amount to one should settle the matter, and yet in many hard cases a modest improvement to one career leaves the choice exactly as difficult as it was. That insensitivity suggests the two are not being measured on a common scale at all, so no amount of information would produce a ranking. Critics reply that our uncertainty is being mistaken for indeterminacy in the values themselves. What follows if the argument succeeds is not paralysis. A choice between incomparable options is not irrational merely because no reason settles it, and the agent who commits to one and makes it her own has done nothing wrong. What is lost is the assurance that a correct answer was available, and some philosophers regard that loss as a truthful description of moral life rather than as a defect in the theory reporting it.

subject: 기근과 이주의 역사적 연쇄
title: Famine and the movements that followed
content: Famine appears in the historical record as a natural disaster, and the accounts written at the time usually blame the weather. Modern study of these episodes has shifted attention to what stood between a poor harvest and mass death, because the same shortfall produced very different outcomes in different places. Regions with stored grain, functioning markets, and rulers willing to release reserves suffered hardship; regions without them suffered catastrophe. The failure was rarely of food alone. What often followed was migration on a scale that reshaped the receiving regions as much as the afflicted ones. People left in the direction of whatever institutions still functioned, and the settlements that absorbed them acquired labour, skills, and conflicts they had not asked for. The historical records of such movements are usually written by the receiving side, which is why they emphasize disorder and say little about what the migrants had left. Historians accordingly read famine as a test of arrangements rather than as an event in itself. Where the machinery of storage and distribution held, the crisis produced a hard year that the sources barely mention; where it failed, the same weather produced a demographic break that is visible in the records for generations. That contrast is the reason the causes of famine are now sought in institutions rather than in the harvest alone.

subject: 이성과 감정의 도덕적 역할
title: Reason and feeling in moral judgment
content: A long tradition in moral philosophy holds that reason discovers what is right and that emotion, being unstable and partial, must be governed by it. An opposing tradition holds that reason alone can establish no value at all, and that our moral judgments rest ultimately on what we care about. The dispute is not merely academic, since each view recommends a different response when feeling and argument conflict. Evidence from psychology has complicated both positions rather than settling between them. People reach moral verdicts quickly and construct their justifications afterward, which supports the second tradition. Yet those verdicts are revisable by argument, and individuals whose emotional responses are impaired reason about moral cases in ways that strike others as monstrous, which supports the first. Neither faculty appears to work properly without the other. The position most philosophers now defend treats emotion as a form of perception rather than an obstacle to judgment. On this account feeling directs attention to what matters in a situation, and reason examines whether the response it prompts can be sustained. A judgment reached without feeling has missed the morally relevant features; one that resists all examination has mistaken a reaction for a reason. The truth in each tradition survives, and what is abandoned is the assumption that either faculty could do the work alone.

subject: 개념은 어떻게 경계를 갖는가
title: How concepts get their boundaries
content: Most of the words we reason with have no sharp edges. A heap remains a heap when one grain is removed, and yet repeating that step must eventually leave something that is not a heap, so the concept cannot be governed by any precise rule. Philosophers call this vagueness, and it is not an occasional defect of careless language but a general feature of the terms we use to describe the world. Several responses have been developed. One holds that vague terms do have precise boundaries which we happen not to know, so a single grain does make the difference and our ignorance conceals it. This preserves classical logic at the cost of a claim most people find incredible. Another response denies that vague statements are simply true or false, admitting intermediate values and revising logic accordingly. A third treats vagueness as arising from the many ways a term could be made precise, and counts a statement as true when it holds on every such way. Each proposal solves the puzzle by giving up something we would rather keep, whether that is a plausible view about meaning or a familiar principle of reasoning. That pattern is itself informative. It suggests that our concepts were built for practical discrimination rather than for the demands that formal argument places on them, and the paradox arises where the two purposes come apart.
